chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I heard him say: 'The one who performs i'tikaf in Mecca may pray in whichever of its houses he wishes; it is the same for him whether he prays in the Mosque or in its houses.' And he said: 'I'tikaf is not valid elsewhere except in the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) or in a mosque of the congregation. And the one performing i'tikaf does not pray in a house other than the mosque in which he has performed i'tikaf, except in Mecca, for he performs i'tikaf in Mecca wherever he wishes, because all of it is the Sanctuary of Allah. And the one performing i'tikaf does not leave the mosque except for a need.'

His saying (peace be upon him): 'for he performs i'tikaf in Mecca wherever he wishes' — he means by it that he prays the prayer of i'tikaf. Do you not see that he began by explaining the prayer of the one performing i'tikaf, saying: 'And the one performing i'tikaf does not pray in a house other than the mosque in which he has performed i'tikaf, except in Mecca, for he performs i'tikaf in Mecca wherever he wishes'? If the meaning were not what we mentioned, it would not be appropriate to except it from the ruling of prayer, and the second statement would not be connected to the first. The estimation of the statement is as we said: 'And the one performing i'tikaf does not pray in a house other than the mosque in which he has performed i'tikaf, except in Mecca, for he prays in a house other than the mosque in which he has performed i'tikaf in it.' And by this it is distinguished from other places.
ai.seo_question: What are the differences between i'tikaf rules in Mecca versus other places according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to clarify the jurisprudential distinction between Mecca and other regions regarding i'tikaf. The text explains that while i'tikaf elsewhere is strictly confined to a specific mosque, Mecca's status as Allah's sanctuary allows the retreatant to pray in any dwelling, a nuance derived from the grammatical context of the verse. This ruling highlights the unique spiritual geography of Mecca in Shia fiqh, where the entire city is considered a single expansive mosque for the purpose of worship.
